Iowa Braces for Blast
The US Army is
set to detonate
68 barrels of unstable lead explosives at a facility in southeastern Iowa this morning, following days of debate involving President Donald Trump, federal courts, environmental groups, and local authorities.
The decision follows a late Monday appeals court ruling that the government has established sufficient safeguards—including physical barriers and air modeling—to limit the spread of toxic lead dust, which is
especially dangerous
to children and pregnant women. The Army says the decades-old explosives have degraded significantly since changes were first detected during routine inspections in March. Officials warn the risk of an uncontrolled explosion will increase as temperatures drop, making immediate action necessary. A controlled open detonation of this scale is unprecedented in US history.
Residents within five miles of the facility have been urged to evacuate until at least Friday. Others are advised to shelter indoors, as the dust could travel up to 100 miles depending on wind conditions.

She Heard Her Daughter Crying … It Was AI
An Arizona mother told local news in 2023 that she got a call and heard what sounded like her 15-year-old daughter, crying and pleading for help. Then a man demanded a ransom. There was no kidnapping. The voice had been cloned by artificial intelligence. It's a frightening example of the kinds of scam calls
Guardio is built to block

State of the House Races
Tennessee’s Victoria Broderick (D)
unseated
Three House races remain uncalled as of this writing. Early voting begins this week for
Louisiana runoff elections
in the state’s 5th and 6th congressional districts; those elections are scheduled for Dec. 12. Meanwhile, a recount for Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District is scheduled to begin Nov. 30, with challenger Jake Johnson (D) leading incumbent Rep. Brad Finstad (R) by 321 votes. All three remaining House races were in districts that President Donald Trump carried in 2024.
The nine states that recently redrew their congressional maps will send at least 16 more Democrats to Congress than in the last election cycle, despite creating a net of nine new districts favoring Republicans. Learn more about how middecade redistricting has
panned out so far
